Economic theory suggests the dominant strategy is to bid my true value of $46. This is because:
1. Bidding less risks losing the item when I value it highly
2. Bidding more than my value guarantees a loss
3. Bidding exactly my value maximizes potential profit
4. Since values are independently drawn, past rounds are irrelevant
5. The second-price auction mechanism incentivizes honest bidding

Economic theory suggests bidding exactly at my private value ($17) is the dominant strategy. This eliminates the risk of overbidding and losing money, while preventing potential underbidding and missing out on winning. Since values are randomly drawn each round and independent, there's no strategic advantage to deviating from bidding my true value. I'll bid precisely $17 to maximize potential profit.

Economic theory suggests bidding exactly my private value ($28) is the dominant strategy in a first-price sealed bid auction. By bidding my true value, I maximize my potential profit - if I win, I'll earn the difference between my value and the second-highest bid. Bidding below my value risks losing the item, while bidding above risks paying more than the item's worth to me. With no prior round history, a straightforward true-value bid seems optimal.
